title: Autumn 2026 Editorial Section 1
abstract: It is with a sense of urgency and hope that we present this special issue of Perspectives in Education. The idea for this collection emerged from the Education Deans’ Forum Colloquium held in Kempton Mark on 17 May 2024. During this gathering, scholars from across South Africa reflected on the alarming findings of the 2023 Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS), which revealed that many Grade 4 learners are unable to read for meaning. This literacy crisis is not merely a policy concern; it affects millions of children whose educational opportunities are constrained by language barriers and limited access to effective literacy instruction.

title: Advancing multilingualism and African language teaching in rural early childhood classrooms through professional development
abstract: Promoting multilingualism and strengthening African language teaching in early childhood classrooms remains a significant challenge in rural South African schools, where teachers often face resource shortages, overcrowded classrooms, and limited professional development opportunities. This study explored how professional development in digital tools may support multilingual pedagogical practices in early childhood education. The research formed part of a three-year engaged scholarship project led by a comprehensive open distance e-learning (CODeL) institution, which collaborated with three Grade 2 teachers from a rural, under-resourced primary school. Teachers participated in professional development workshops focused on using artificial intelligence (AI) tools, specifically Canva and ChatGPT, to design multilingual literacy resources. Through this process, teachers developed a large multilingual “big book” used for shared reading in the classroom across several languages, including an African home language and English. The study adopted a qualitative case study approach within an interpretivist paradigm. Data were generated through teacher reflections, workshop observations, and a

title: Translanguaging in action: Foundation phase learners’ use of different communicative linguistic resources for meaning-making during science education
abstract: This study explores how primary school learners in a multilingual South African foundation phase classroom use linguistic resources during communicative exchanges in science experiments. Focusing on the topic living and non-living things, it examines how plurilingual learners creatively draw on linguistic and cultural resources to engage in science explorations. Employing an ethnographic research design, the study involved 20 participants (one Grade 3 teacher and 19 learners aged 8–10 years). Ethnographically informed, the study collected data through video recordings and classroom interactions in a third-grade class (8–10-year-olds) to analyse their participation in both whole-class discussions and small-group interactions. Data were analysed using conversation analysis, informed by a critical ethnographic lens. This analysis considers how learners construct and communicate meaning as they interact in diverse groups. The findings reveal the importance of dialogical, open-ended classroom spaces that allow linguistically and culturally diverse learners to draw on their unique resources, enabling them to participate more fully in science discussions. title: Promoting African languages through play-based learning in early childhood education
abstract: The Department of Education’s Language in Education Policy supports mother tongue instruction in the early grades, emphasising African languages. The importance of strong mother tongue instruction leads this study to explore play-based pedagogy to enhance African language skills among Grade R learners. Play-based pedagogy centres on play’s central role in teaching and learning. It helps children make sense of their world and adapt to new situations. Guided by Vygotsky’s social learning theory, the study investigated teachers’ perceptions of play-based learning to promote mother tongue instruction in Mpumalanga province. The research question was: How can play-based learning support African languages and the holistic language development of young children? This qualitative study, set within an interpretivist paradigm, included five purposively selected Grade R teachers. These teachers participated in semi-structured interviews and classroom observations. The findings show teachers commonly use play-based strategies such as songs, storytelling, rhymes, and games. These activities encourage spontaneous use of African languages and support both language acquisition and holistic develop

title: Using the discussion method to improve the ability of Korean learners to write narrative texts in Indonesian
abstract: Instructional methodology is known to influence the efficacy of foreign language teaching and learning. This study aimed to investigate the effect of using the discussion method to teach narrative text writing to foreign language students. Two groups of South Korean-speaking students who were enrolled in the Indonesian Language for Foreign Speakers programme (BIPA Level 6) participated in the study, which was conducted using a non-equivalent control group design. The discussion method was used to teach narrative text writing in Indonesian to students in the experimental group, whereas students in the control group learned narrative text writing by listening and taking notes. The ability of the students to write narrative text in Indonesian before and after narrative-test-writing instruction was assessed using data collected by administering pre-tests and post-tests to both groups. The results showed that whereas all the students benefited from narrative-text-writing instruction, learning through discussion had a greater positive effect on the BIPA Level 6 learners’ ability to write narrative text in Indonesian than learning by listening and taking notes. title: A linguistic analysis of spelling errors in Northern Sotho-speaking Grade 3learners: A cross-sectional approach
abstract: Spelling ability is a crucial determinant of academic achievement and an integral part of the writing process. It is a complex cognitive-linguistic skill that requires knowledge of letter sound correspondence, phonological awareness, orthographic awareness, and morphological awareness. Despite its importance, research on spelling development in Southern Bantu languages, particularly in Northern Sotho, is still sparse. This study examines the linguistic patterns underlying spelling errors made by Northern Sotho-speaking Grade 3 children, providing a detailed linguistic analysis of error types. Data were collected from 106 Northern Sotho-speaking children using an age-appropriate real-word spelling task that included words of varying complexity. This study explores how Northern Sotho’s agglutinative and disjunctive structure may influence spelling acquisition, particularly in relation to learners’ developing phonological, orthographic, and morphological awareness. A preliminary analysis was conducted to determine some of the spelling errors made by learners at the end of Grade 3. Examples of errors made by children in Northern Sotho included substitution (e.g., kg in kgona ‘be able’

title: AI-driven cultural fluency in isiZulu: Harnessing artificial intelligence to empower indigenous language education
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomous learning systems has transformed language education worldwide. However, most studies have focused on well-resourced languages such as English, Spanish, French, and Mandarin, with limited attention to African indigenous and under-resourced languages, such as isiZulu. This study interrogates the use of autonomous language-learning technologies in isiZulu, exploring how adaptive digital tools and AI-driven methodologies can support learner autonomy, enhance cultural relevance, and promote linguistic proficiency, particularly through the interpretation of idioms and proverbs. Drawing on secondary literature on computer assisted language learning (CALL), narrative studies of AI in language education, and emerging research on distributed agency in second language teaching, the study examines both the potential opportunities and inherent challenges of deploying autonomous systems in isiZulu education. It further discusses the need for culturally responsive pedagogies, teacher professional development, and appropriate technological adaptations. The study concludes with recommendations for future research and policy implic

title: Navigating uncertainty:Pre‑service foundation phase teachers ’reflections on readiness to teach reading
abstract: South Africa faces a major challenge in improving early literacy instruction, as reading proficiency in the foundation phase is essential for later academic success. Research shows that after three years of schooling, 81% of learners cannot read for meaning in any of the country’s 12 official languages, and eight out of 10 children require support to achieve expected reading outcomes. Poor teaching quality and weaknesses in initial teacher education programmes are key contributing factors. Studies indicate that many primary school teachers have low expectations of learners and provide limited support to struggling readers, leaving preservice teachers underprepared to teach literacy effectively. This mixed-methods study explored how pre-service foundation phase teachers perceived their preparedness to teach reading and identified areas of reading instruction requiring greater emphasis in teacher education programmes. The study involved 68 final year Bachelor of Education foundation phase students at a South African higher education institution. Data were collected through questionnaires and focus group discussions and analysed using pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) and the framew

title: English second language teaching and learning andChatGPT: Perspectives of university lecturers in Namibia
abstract: The research explored how ChatGPT could support English as a second language (ESL) teaching and learning in Namibia’s public universities, drawing on insights from lecturers at the University of Namibia (UNAM) and the Namibia University of Science and Technology (NUST). Guided by a constructivist philosophy, the study adopted a qualitative case study strategy with a descriptive exploratory research design. The population comprised English communication lecturers, and purposive sampling was used to select 20 lecturers teaching English communication skills modules at these universities. Data were collected via open-ended questionnaires and were analysed thematically. Findings reveal that while lecturers acknowledge ChatGPT’s pedagogical affordances, such as grammar correction, summarisation, vocabulary development, and idea generation, its integration is constrained by ethical concerns, student overreliance on AI-generated content, limited digital literacy among educators, the absence of institutional policies, and infrastructural challenges. The findings suggest that ChatGPT should be applied as a supplementary mechanism within ESL teaching, working alongside the indispensable human

title: The second language paradox: Bridging policy and pedagogy using results from large-scale assessment studies
abstract: The racialised history of South African education, rooted in colonial and apartheid policies, has deliberately marginalised indigenous languages while privileging English and Afrikaans. This legacy still shapes current educational inequities. Despite post-apartheid policies that mandate mother-tongue instruction in the foundation phase, a large percentage of learners continue to demonstrate low levels of language proficiency. The gap between policy intent and classroom reality can be attributed to historical inequities, the perceived economic benefits of English, and assessment systems that prioritise performance and curriculum coverage over learning. Collectively, these factors create what we term the second language paradox. This paradox poses core challenges for improving teaching and learning in the Foundation phase. However, teachers and education officials lack targeted information to identify and address specific learning and teaching challenges. Without this information, appropriate classroom decisions and informed system interventions cannot be adequately made. title: Critical literacy as a humanising strategy in the isiXhosa literacy curriculum
abstract: Literacy teaching and learning encompass reading and writing and foster critical engagement with texts that have cultural and social implications. This understanding of literacy teaching has motivated me to critically engage with student teachers to promote social justice and understand how language empowers people to engage meaningfully in their social world. The purpose of this self-study is to explore my experiences of teaching critical literacy as a pedagogy in the isiXhosa literacy curriculum in the Bachelor of Education programme at a South African university. I used an art-based self-study methodology and Dewey’s reflective practice theory to examine my own teaching practices through a socio-cultural lens. My observations and interpretations were documented in reflective journal entries and collage-making as data-gathering methods. It allowed me to reflect, clarify, and critique my own psychological and cognitive processes and my resulting teaching approach, based on my understanding that critical literacy can empower me to develop insight into texts and the social constructs embedded therein. It is therefore key for teacher education programmes to engage in reflexive practi

title: A Setswana translation and adaptation of the Stark Griffin™ Dyslexia screening test
abstract: South African learners, particularly in Grade 4, demonstrate significant challenges in reading comprehension. The 2021 PIRLS study found that 81% of these learners could not read with comprehension. Notably, even Setswana-speaking learners, who receive initial instruction in their home language, struggle. It seems that factors beyond the medium of instruction, such as the development of indigenous languages and equitable resource distribution, are crucial. The shift to English-medium instruction in the intermediate phase further exacerbates the problem, making it challenging to diagnose reading difficulties, especially in second language learners, accurately. Linguistic disparities, encompassing phonetic, phonological, morphological, and orthographic differences and challenges in phonological awareness, contribute to these difficulties and hinder the identification of specific learning disorders, such as developmental dyslexia. Critically, South African standardised screening tools for developmental dyslexia (DD) are only available in English, leaving English second-language speakers, such as Setswana learners, without adequate diagnostic support. To address this gap, this study fo

title: Examining critical thinking and creativity in second language classrooms in South African higher education
abstract: This study examines how second-language instruction in South African higher education can be strengthened to foster critical thinking and creativity in multilingual, structurally unequal learning environments. Positioned within broader debates surrounding 21st-century competencies, the study explores how pedagogical practices, institutional structures, and technological systems shape opportunities for learner participation, critical engagement, and creative expression. Framed by socio-cultural theory and the design justice framework, the study critically examines how linguistic hierarchies, curricular rigidity, unequal digital access, and exclusionary educational practices continue to shape second language learning in South Africa and the broader Global South. The study adopted a systematic literature review methodology guided by the PRISMA framework to synthesise interdisciplinary scholarship published between 2017 and 2025 and sourced from multiple academic databases, and analysed using thematic synthesis. Comparative insights from India, Brazil, China, Kenya, and other Global South contexts were incorporated to examine emerging approaches to curriculum reform, project-based lear

title: Reshaping the landscape of language education: Sharing insights, best practices, and research
abstract: Over the past decade, we have witnessed a massive shift in information and digital technologies that has had an enormous impact on second language teaching and learning. These changes have forced education to undergo significant transformations in how languages are taught and mediated. The rapid pace of technological advancement, the increasing importance of global communication, and the evolving needs of learners are reshaping the landscape of language education. Despite these advancements, there remains a gap in understanding how best to integrate these emerging tools and methodologies into effective language instruction. Educators, researchers, and policymakers continue to seek answers to critical questions about how to prepare learners to thrive in an interconnected, digital world.

title: Minister’s privilege: A response to the 2023PIRLS results
abstract: This paper responds to the 2023 release of the PIRLS results, which, yet again, highlights the existing literacy crisis within the South African basic education system, affecting the entire education system from the foundational to the tertiary levels. Learners who fail to transition from decoding to comprehension by the end of Grade 3 rarely catch up, often struggle academically and eventually fail, reducing their access to socio-economic success. Despite the South African Minister of Education’s assertion that what is needed is more time, this paper uses empirical data from two studies, one conducted before PIRLS and the other after, to illustrate that learners continue to have reading levels well below expectations, both in their home languages and in English. Furthermore, teachers lack the training and knowledge needed to address these challenges, focusing on teacher-led classroom interactions and decoding at the expense of comprehension. However, evidence suggests that approaches such as learning to read, reading to learn and translanguaging may assist in facilitating reading development through extended learning, meaningful interactions, and increased learner engagement, resu

title: Editorial Summer 2025
abstract: Early childhood education (ECE) lays the foundation for a child's lifelong learning journey. More and more, new insights and understandings of child development are evolving, and concomitantly, new preschool education has seen several exciting trends in recent years, with innovative approaches to enhance children's learning experiences. Current trends in early childhood education, inter alia, focus on increasing physical activity, social-emotional learning (SEL), inclusive classrooms, integrating STEM/STEAM through play-based methods, a heightened focus on mental health, outdoor activity, and holistic development requiring higher degrees for educators, and incorporating more technology into learning. In this section of Perspectives in Education, we explore the latest trends and developments shaping the landscape of early childhood education.

title: Place-based education: enhancing equity and sustainability in early childhood development
abstract: South Africa is a signatory to United Nations (UN) treaties on sustainable development (SD) and has endorsed the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UNSDGs). Early childhood development (ECD) is central to SD and is also considered a fundamental human right in South Africa. This centrality is premised on recognising that comprehensive ECD benefits both the individual and the South African society by addressing key challenges such as inequity and inclusion. Hence, the National Integrated Early Childhood Development Policy (NIECDP) (2015) was promulgated. The South African ECD context is plagued with inequalities, and a lack of equitable and inclusive access to quality education increases injustices experienced within the ECD sector. This results in environments with little educational stimulation and poor-quality ECD programmes. These insufficiencies not only negatively impact the cognitive development of young children and their skills and educational attainment, but they also jeopardise the country’s vision of SD. This article proposes place based education (PBE) as an educational approach to address educational disparities in ECD, and to create the equitable, inclusive

title: Leading with heart: Empowering foundation phase teachers with values-driven leadership in times of crisis
abstract: In times of crisis, it is not policies but people-guided by empathy, respect, and gratitude, who sustain schools. This study investigates how school leaders in one private, one urban public and one rural public school in South Africa used values-driven leadership, conceptualised here as leading with heart, the leadership rooted in empathy, gratitude and human connection, support foundation phase teachers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Adopting a qualitative, interpretivist design, the study further explores leadership challenges linked to the rapid transition to online learning while maintaining teacher morale. Data were collected through interviews, observations, document analysis and reflective journals with 35 participants, including departmental officials, principals, teachers and parents. Findings reveal that gratitude and empathy significantly enhanced teacher resilience. While private schools expressed appreciation through praise and small tokens, urban public schools offered inconsistent support with limited personal recognition. In contrast, rural public schools cultivated a strong sense of understanding and gratitude despite resource constraints. The study underscores the

title: Positioning young children as capable beings in informal settlement early childhood development centres
abstract: Traditional teaching methods often overlook young children’s active role in learning, thereby limiting their voices as agents in their own development. This qualitative research study explores how early childhood development (ECD) practitioners position young children as active beings in their own learning experiences. Grounded in constructivist and sociocultural theoretical frameworks and drawing on participatory action learning and action research methodologies, the study enabled four university researchers to collaborate with six ECD practitioners in examining pedagogical approaches that support children’s agency. The participants engaged in three research cycles using dialogues and forum group discussions to express their perspectives on enabling young children as capable beings in their learning journey. The collaborative nature of the study ensured a comprehensive understanding of children’s participation in educational contexts. The findings revealed multifaceted strategies to position young children as active participants and to demonstrate profound respect for their views. Through open-ended questioning techniques, practitioners created meaningful spaces for children to ar

title: Building the workforce for an early childhood home-visiting programme: Reflections from the field
abstract: This article explores the experiences of a group of community members working at a local nongovernmental organisation who attended and participated in an early childhood development (ECD) home-visiting training workshop. The participants werepurposively selected as they were already working as community health workers and life-skills coordinators in two communities ofthe Eastern Cape, South Africa. The communities are informal settlements characterised by extreme poverty, rendering manyyoung children in the communities vulnerable to risk factors and poor future outcomes. A qualitative approach, grounded in aninterpretivist paradigm and an intervention research design, was adopted to evaluate the implementation of an early childhoodhome-visiting programme for vulnerable children aged 0–2 years. This article presents the findings on the second researchobjective of the broader study: to explore the effectiveness of a transdisciplinary early childhood home-visiting training programme.A multidisciplinary team comprising professionals from across education, health, and social work conducted the training. Datawere generated using focus group discussions and analysed using thematic analysi

title: Collaborative approaches to support school readiness through movement play: Insights from South Africa
abstract: Globally, concerns about increasingly sedentary lifestyles have highlighted the importance of play-based learning and physical activity. Although physical development is regarded as an essential aspect of school readiness, many factors at home and at school seem to be keeping young children from engaging in physically active play. Considering the associated educational outcomes and holistic development related to school readiness, there is a need for greater focus on movement and play at home and at school, and for partnerships to facilitate these activities. This paper emanates from a doctoral study that explored the way parents and teachers can collaborate to facilitate the development of fundamental skills through play-based movement activities. Then study was conducted in a low-socio-economic community in the Northern Cape, South Africa, with eight participants. Mezirow’s transformative learning theory served as the theoretical framework to explore more inclusive frames of reference. A participatory action learning and action research design was implemented, using arts based methods and discussions to generate data. Data analysis was conducted using Braun and Clarke’s recursive

title: Exploring storytelling methodologies on childhood development: A collaborative study with early childhood education practitioners in rural settings
abstract: Storytelling has long been recognised as a powerful tool inearly childhood education, captivating children’s imaginationswhile fostering essential developmental skills. This qualitativestudy explored how storytelling techniques enhanced cognitive,emotional, and social development among young children at a preschoolin the rural community of Siyabuswa, Mpumalanga, SouthAfrica. Mavuba Pre-school is a pseudonym assigned to protect theidentity and anonymity of the participating school.The study involved seven practitioners and twenty children,focusing on integrating storytelling into daily teaching practicesto create more engaging and compelling learning experiences.Grounded in Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory, which highlightsthe role of language and social interaction in learning, the studyemployed a participatory action research (PAR) approach. Thisapproach enabled practitioners to serve as co-researchers, sharing their experiences, challenges, and insights as they collaboratively refined storytelling techniques. title: Community participation pathways for sustainability in early childhood education. A systematic review
abstract: EEducational communities serve as vital environments where children develop meaningful relationships and acquire essential knowledge regarding sustainability. Nonetheless, the extant literature on early childhood education for sustainability (ECEfS) has addressed the collective participation of these communities in a fragmented fashion, frequently overlooking the relationships among diverse stakeholders. This systematic review analyses studies published between 2015 and 2024 that adhere to PRISMA guidelines, aiming to foster dialogue on participatory approaches involving children, early childhood practitioners, families, and the educational experiences resulting from this collective engagement. The selected studies were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, which recognised a consistent acknowledgement of children’s agency and the mediating role of early childhood practitioners in promoting collective learning. Conversely, family participation often remains marginal, with limited influence on the design and decision-making processes. Similarly, educational experiences tend to focus on environmental activities mainly within educational institutions, revealing a gap between par

title: Policy imperatives for enhancing parental involvement in inclusive rural foundation phase education
abstract: Parental involvement plays a crucial role in the social, emotional, and academic development of children, particularly in inclusive rural Foundation Phase classes. However, in rural areas, teachers often face challenges working with learners of varied abilities, especially when parents are not actively involved in their children's education. This lack of involvement hinders the effectiveness of teaching and learning, which can be exacerbated by limited resources in rural inclusive schools. The purpose of this study is to explore the significance of parental involvement as a strategy to support children in inclusive rural Foundation Phase classes. It seeks to understand how teachers can effectively engage parents, despite obstacles such as poverty, unemployment, low literacy levels, and geographic barriers, which all contribute to reduced parental involvement. The study is underpinned by Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Systems Theory and Bourdieu’s Social Capital Theory. These frameworks provide insight into the complex dynamics that influence parental involvement and the potential for parents to act as vital support systems for their children’s education. title: In memory of Prof Ewelina Kinga Niemczyk (5 September 1973 – 18 October 2025)
abstract: It is with sincere, heartfelt sadness that the Editorial Team of Perspectives in Education has learnt of the passing of our beloved and respected colleague, Prof Ewelina Kinga Niemczyk at the age of 52. Born on 5 September 1973, Prof Niemczyk died on October 18th, 2025 from multiple complications associated with glioblastoma, a highly invasive glioma in the brain.

title: Innovative approaches to sustainable quality teaching in early childhood development: A scoping review of assessment criteria in resource-limited environments
abstract: In South Africa, there is an urgent need for sustainable, quality teaching in early childhood development. The ability to understand different styles and approaches is crucial for fostering a critical and reflective attitude towards teaching and care. Early childhood development (ECD) should be guided by children’s natural interests rather than imposed by rigid curricula or external expectations. This phase should be a time for the learner to unfold, connect, listen, and understand, while creating an inclusive community of learners that welcomes diversity and celebrates culture and tradition. The Global Education Monitoring Report (GEM) emphasises the need for novel approaches to teaching, with an urgent focus on achieving the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 4 (quality education). This approach requires a shift in our thinking about teaching. Higher education plays a key role in this transformation, as early childhood development degrees must embrace sustainable education as a platform to support children and families. title: Critical diversity literacy for inclusion in early childhood care and education
abstract: Applying critical diversity literacy (CDL) in early childhood care and education (ECCE) settings provides essential tools for teachers to navigate and address the complexities of diversity during this formative developmental period. This study explores how CDL can be adopted to promote genuine inclusion in ECCE settings, addressing a significant gap in research on CDL in ECCE contexts. Underpinned by Critical Pedagogy, this research employs a participatory action learning and action research (PALAR) design that centres teacher voice and experience. Through activities such as the Power Flower and the Privilege Game, ECCE teachers and trainers engaged in critical reflection about their social positioning and implicit biases that impact classroom practices. Drawing from a wider study on inclusion, data were generated for this article from reflective journals. Data analysis reveals that CDL activities lead to greater introspection about hierarchical power relations and the intersectionality of various identity markers. Coresearchers developed awareness of how contemporary systems of oppression pervade current educational spaces and the crucial role of language in perpetuating or challe

title: Transformative pedagogy: Harnessing constructivist and participatory approaches to foster learner engagement and effective instruction
abstract: Innovative and participatory pedagogical approaches have emerged as transformative strategies in modern education, fostering active learner engagement and reshaping classroom dynamics. Grounded in constructivist learning theories, particularly those proposed by Piaget and Vygotsky, these approaches position learners as active participants in constructing their own knowledge. This paper explores the impact of these pedagogies, focusing on methods such as inquiry-based learning, cooperative learning, and the integration of digital tools to create interactive and inclusive learning environments. Drawing on social constructivism as a theoretical framework, the paper demonstrates how participatory pedagogies empower learners to take ownership of their learning, develop critical thinking skills, and collaborate more effectively. According to Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD), learners benefit most when they engage in tasks just beyond their current abilities, facilitated by guidance from teachers or peers. This framework highlights the teacher's role as a facilitator, guiding learners through experiential learning processes that promote deeper understanding and knowledge rete

title: Green Songs as music education for sustainable development in an early childhood setting: Tuning into pre-service music teacher voices
abstract: development (ESD) into music teacher education using the Green Songs Project, an undergraduate service-learning project in a music education module. Seven pre-service music teachers (PSMTs) composed and taught original environmental songs to pre-schoolers to foster ecological awareness through music. In this qualitative case study, I analysed the PSMTs’ journal reflections on the project, my observations, and our discussions exploring their experiences and the meanings they ascribed to writing and teaching green songs to pre-schoolers. We also discussed how the project could promote music education for sustainable development (MESD) in an early childhood setting. Five themes were generated, indicating that MESD can be promoted by 1) using movement and song to teach and learn about conservation; 2) integrating a mixture of excitement, laughter, and enthusiasm; 3) creating opportunities to make the world a better place to live in; 4) remembering things that impact our lives and 5) developing consistent, encouraging teaching strategies to foster learning and development for MESD. title: Editorial 1
abstract: Perspectives in Education (PIE) aims to promote meaningful dialogue and scholarly exchange on current issues in education, including teaching and learning, educational leadership, policy and learner development across diverse developmental stages and contexts. Building on this focus, this special issue foregrounds important discussions on early childhood education for sustainable development in Southern Africa, aimed at addressing the research question: “How can the quality of early childhood education for sustainable development be enhanced through participatory research in resource-constrained environments for children from birth to nine years?” Against the backdrop of Southern Africa’s socioeconomic inequalities, the collection of articles foregrounds early childhood as a critical entry point for advancing sustainability. Across the contributions, a clear and consistent theme emerges: High quality, sustainable early childhood education depends on strong partnerships, context responsive pedagogies, the recognition of children’s rights, agency and diverse needs, as well as a well supported workforce. These elements form the backbone of sustainable development in early learning sys

title: The role of higher education in the development of financial literacy skills of small business owners in South Africa
abstract: South Africa faces a critically high unemployment rate due to poor educational attainments and socio-economic disadvantages. The critical need for job creation demands a renewed look at entrepreneurial endeavours. Higher education institutions (HEIs) are critical in producing knowledge for society. Innovative ways of supporting entrepreneurial learning are required to bridge the financial knowledge gap of educationally marginalised socio-economic groups, such as small business owners from impoverished communities. The study aimed to gain insights into the perceptions of small business owners and ascertain the role of HEIs in developing financial literacy skills of small businesses. Data was collected from twelve small business owners who participated in a two-day financial literacy workshop. A phenomenological and mixed-method approach was applied to gather quantitative and qualitative data through questionnaires. Challenges faced by small business owners and the dire need for financial literacy were identified, suggesting an urgent role for HEIs to equip small business owners with the tools necessary to run their businesses effectively. title: A conceptual framework for early childhood science education for global citizenship education: An indigenous lens
abstract: Our study presents a theoretical exploration and conceptual framework designed to integrate indigenous knowledge systems (IKS) into early childhood science education to foster global citizenship education among children. We propose a culturally responsive and theoretically grounded model explicitly tailored to the South African context through a comprehensive review and synthesis of existing literature, theoretical perspectives, and best practices across early childhood education, IKS, and global citizenship education (GCE). Early childhood science education is vital in nurturing children’s curiosity, world understanding, and cognitive skills such as critical thinking and problem-solving. However, the lack of practical pedagogical approaches and curriculum designs highlights the need for innovative theoretical frameworks. Employing a narrative literature review methodology, our conceptual paper draws on peer-reviewed sources from 2000 to 2025, selected through keyword searches in databases like Scopus and Google Scholar. Data were synthesised through thematic analysis to inform the framework’s development, with inclusion criteria focusing on early learning and curriculum transforma

title: Re-imagining early childhood education: A Freirean critique of eco-pedagogy’s absence in South Africa’s foundation phase
abstract: The escalating ecological crisis demands a rethinking of early childhood education, particularly within South Africa’s Foundation phase. This paper presents a conceptual analysis that draws on Paulo Freire’s critical pedagogy, eco-pedagogy, and play-based learning theories to examine the absence of eco-pedagogical practices in current curricula. Despite the Curriculum and Assessment Policy Statement (CAPS) including elements of environmental awareness, its treatment remains largely fact-based and disconnected from learners’ lived experiences. We argue that this approach reinforces a “banking” education model, limiting opportunities for children to develop ecological consciousness and agency. As a theoretical contribution, this paper proposes a framework for embedding play-based eco-pedagogy within the constraints of CAPS by: (a) integrating experiential activities such as nature walks, gardening, and environmental storytelling into life skills; (b) using guided play to link ecological concepts with literacy and numeracy outcomes; and (c) encouraging teachers to adopt dialogical, inquiry-driven practices that connect classroom content with local environmental realities. title: Establishing a structured mentoring programme for early-career staff at a South African research-intensive university
abstract: In this paper, I share my experience establishing a structured mentoring programme to benefit early-career academics and support staff at a research-intensive university in South Africa. In justifying the adopted process, the paper first clarifies what mentoring is and is not in higher education. It further justifies the benefits and importance of a structured mentoring programme in this chosen context. While the institution provides many support programmes, especially for academic staff, equal participation for all staff is yet to be realised. This autoethnographic qualitative analysis employs Nancy Fraser’s normative framework on social justice to explain how the programme was established to foster a socially just workplace and encourage participatory parity. The programme participants included three groups of permanent employees: those employed through the nGAP, other early-career academic staff, and early-career academic support staff. These groups had unequal access to career development resources. Mentors for the programme were recruited from lecturers who had completed the nGAP, while mentees were chosen based on recommendations from heads of departments (HODs). An 18-month

title: Lessons learnt and insights shared: The Diagnostic Mathematics Information for Student Retention and Success (DMISRS) Case Studies Dialogue on teaching first-year mathematics in South Africa
abstract: The Diagnostic Mathematics Information for Student Retention and Success (DMISRS) project was a collaborative project focused on first-year mathematics, which drew together lecturers in South African higher education institutions and other related organisations. Various themes were explored during the annual DMISRS symposia from 2018 to 2022. The project’s culmination was a final DMISRS symposium held in November 2023, which focused on the case studies that examine the sub-projects that have emerged over the years. The symposia have tackled critical themes, including collaborative practices and courses that influence graduation rates, the psychological well-being of students, and innovative solutions in first-year mathematics, such as assessments, performance metrics, blended learning approaches and curriculumdevelopment. The case studies offer valuable narratives of day-to-day interactions, teaching and learning activities, and shared resources or practices in first-year mathematics education experiences. title: Doctoral student attrition in Namibian higher education institutions: An analysis of implications and coping strategies
abstract: Doctoral student attrition poses a significant challenge in higher education, particularly in Namibia, where non-completion rates undermine academic progress, institutional goals and national development agendas. Through the lens of Tinto’s theory of student integration, this article examines the implications of doctoral attrition for individual students and the broader Namibian society, while exploring coping strategies employed by students to navigate academic challenges. Globally, research highlights a concerning trend, with nearly half of doctoral candidates across higher education systems failing to attain their degrees. This article adopts a qualitative approach grounded in an interpretivist framework to explore this phenomenon. Data collection involved semi-structured interviews with 23 doctoral candidates registered at two Namibian universities between 2013 and 2019. Thematic analysis revealed multiple consequences linked to prolonged doctoral study timelines or premature withdrawal, alongside resilience strategies participants utilised to mitigate academic and institutional barriers. title: Exploring classroom interpersonal communication skills of English second language teachers in Nigeria
abstract: The teacher-student relationship is an aspect of classroom interaction that could be developed through interpersonal communication among classroom participants. Fostering such a relationship is the function of a positive and collaborative environment marked with mutual respect, understanding, and friendliness that motivates students’ learning. This paper examined the influence of the interpersonal aspect of teacher-talk on teacherstudent relationships and student verbal participation in classroom interactions in Ekiti State in Nigeria. The study employed a mixedmethods approach, involving both quantitative and qualitative analyses of eight recorded lessons. The findings revealed that all the categories of teacher-talk identified in the study could be used to facilitate effective classroom interpersonal relationships among teacher and learner participants. The interpersonal aspect of teacher-talk only allowed for limited interpersonal relationships between them and the students because the interaction was teacher-biased. title: Towards a conceptual framework for equality in higher education partnerships
abstract: The quest for equality and equity in higher education partnerships is intensifying. Stakeholders, including donor organisations, higher education leaders, and academics, seek a suitable theoretical framework for entrenching equality and equity in externally funded consortia, partnerships and networks. Using legal and social sciences methods and drawing on an online survey of senior international officers and interviews conducted at four institutions as select case studies, we propose a four-dimensional understanding of substantive equality rooted in partnership values as a theoretical framework for equality in higher education partnerships. We demonstrate that it has the potential to transform the discourse and practice of higher education partnerships by ensuring fair resource allocation, affirming the equal worth and dignity, enhancing stakeholder decision-making and transparent communication between institutions and promoting diversity as a driver of transformation. title: Agentic engagement in a South African academic literacies classroom: A case study of student and facilitator experiences
abstract: Agency is central to the success of academic literacies classrooms. Agency manifests through agentic engagement where students take responsibility for their studies, and educators explicitly foster this quality. However, despite the importance of this construct, agentic engagement has not yet been investigated within a Southern African context. This study aimed to fill this gap by exploring agentic engagement in a South African academic literacies programme through the experiences of students and facilitators. A case study was conducted using document analysis, a facilitator focus group discussion, and semi-structured student interviews. Findings from the document analysis indicate that the academic literacies classroom within this programme is conducive to agentic engagement. However, student and facilitator responses indicate that agentic engagement is limited in the studied academic literacies classroom context, despite a favourable classroom environment. The results suggest that agentic engagement manifests in an alternative way in this context, where students prefer to demonstrate peer reciprocity with each other instead of with the facilitator in front of the whole class. title: Investigating the adoption of electronic books for teaching and learning in rural public secondary schools
abstract: Digital transformation has shown remarkable development by digitising traditional books into electronic books or e-books. Various publishing industries and academic libraries globally see e-books as a golden bullet. In addition, most academic libraries widely adopt e-books, scholars and tertiary institution students. However, most rural public secondary schools have a shortage of printed books. Rural public schools, based on literature, are not taking advantage of the availability of e-books because there is low adoption of digital books in these schools. The study investigated how rural public secondary schools use e-books in teaching and learning. To achieve this aim, data were collected from teachers and students from rural public secondary schools using a survey. In addition, IBM SPSS Statistics was used to analyse the collected data. The study has revealed that rural public secondary school teachers and their students are unaware and have little to no knowledge about e-books.
